subject: 92FAB05B93EAEA7C6C668DD0C91ADFB1
introduction: Bahá’u’lláh’s letter to Náṣiri’d-Dín Sháh is a petition: it sets the plea of a persecuted community before the king and asks for an inquiry. This guide gathers that and many smaller acts of the same kind, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s advice on when and how to petition a government (together, calmly, through the proper channel, never so as to inflame), his letters to officials, and the accounts of what such appeals achieved; and it sets beside them the prayers in which the same distress is carried to God. Scripture knows both: Esther going in to the king, Paul’s “I appeal unto Caesar”, the importunate widow; and the Psalms of complaint. Moses before Pharaoh and the three in Babylon are the appeals that did not ask.
questions: What rules for petitioning authority can be drawn from readings 2, 14 and 17? What do they guard against?
Esther pleaded; Moses demanded. When is each right, and which do the readings prefer for a persecuted minority?
The readings ask prayers for the very rulers under whom the Bahá’ís suffered. What does such prayer do to the one who prays?
Why does the guide place petitions to kings and prayers to God together?

outside.why: It is incumbent on me to present the plea of the oppressed before the King. Esther: so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law: and if I perish, I perish.
Have recourse to the government, but not in a way that inflames. Seek the peace of the city, and pray unto the Lord for it.
We beseech the Sovereign to investigate in person. The king’s heart is in the hand of the Lord, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will.
The Sultan should have called Us and investigated. Paul: I stand at Caesar’s judgment seat, where I ought to be judged; I appeal unto Caesar.

Imprisoned in a ruined barracks, women and infants with them. Moses went to his king with a demand, not a plea: let my people go. And Pharaoh said, who is the Lord, that I should obey his voice? Why do the readings choose the petitioner’s tone over the prophet’s?
“In the name of God and humanity we protest.” A widow came to an unjust judge, saying, avenge me of mine adversary; and by her continual coming she wearied him.
“I have risen to mention something of my distress.” How long, O Lord? how long shall mine enemy be exalted over me?
A warning written to Sultan ‘Abdu’l-Ḥamíd. Nathan to David: thou art the man.
Petitioning the centre directly and alone is unwise; when oppression occurs, act together. Be ye wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.
Appeal to no authority but the government. The powers that be are ordained of God.
That God raise up one to carry the message to the king. Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Here am I; send me.

A royal letter and the Báb’s reply. Three subjects to their king: we are not careful to answer thee in this matter; be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods. Where, in the readings, does deference to a ruler end?
Beseech God to assist the Shah, despite all. Prayers be made for kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life.
Prayers for the Sultan’s welfare are necessary. Pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you.

Praying for the Shah is obligatory. The Psalmist’s caution against expecting much: put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help. How do the readings combine loyalty to rulers with reliance on God alone?
A man with a grievance reaches the minister of war. Let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.
“We hear the lamentation of the House: deliver me from the wrongdoing people.” How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge?
What has befallen the believers. By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept.
“Look upon my wretched state.” God be merciful to me a sinner.
Save me from the pit of self and the fire of tyranny. Out of the depths have I cried unto thee, O Lord.
The Refuge of them that flee. God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.
There is none to help me save Thee. My help cometh from the Lord, which made heaven and earth.

shortfall: About sixty readings are routine correspondence about particular petitions, or prayers of supplication in one voice; a companion was set at each distinct step and in three places among the prayers.

acts-i-appeal-unto-caesar.text: Then said Paul, I stand at Caesar's judgment seat, where I ought to be judged: to the Jews have I done no wrong, as thou very well knowest. For if I be an offender, or have committed any thing worthy of death, I refuse not to die: but if there be none of these things whereof these accuse me, no man may deliver me unto them. I appeal unto Caesar
